planting.note: Direct sow once soil has warmed after the last frost date.

directions: This Lebanese-type zucchini produces slightly wider, nutty-flavored fruit on an open, easy-to-pick bush habit. Direct sow after the soil has warmed following the last frost, spacing hills generously since the plant spreads nearly a yard across. Harvest young for the sweetest flavor when roasting, stuffing, or frying; the open habit makes spotting ripe fruit under the leaves easier than with older bush types.

planting.note: Direct sow after the last frost in warm, fertile soil.

directions: Sure Pick is a dark-green zucchini bred for reliability, continuing to set fruit through heat spells and periods of light pollinator activity when other squash plantings stall. Direct sow after the last frost and keep plants picked every couple of days to encourage continued production. Its weather and disease tolerance make it a dependable main-season squash for gardeners in variable climates.

planting.note: Start seed indoors 6-8 weeks before the last frost, then transplant once nights stay reliably warm.

directions: Mesilla is a large New Mexico-style hot pepper bred to be useful at every stage of ripeness, from mild jalapeno-like heat when picked green to a sweeter, more intense flavor once fully red. Start seed indoors 6-8 weeks before the last frost and transplant into warm soil after danger of frost passes. The thick-walled, meaty pods hold up well to roasting, stuffing, and frying.

planting.note: Start seed indoors 6-8 weeks before the last frost; move transplants outside once the weather has warmed.

directions: Orange Pop is a compact snacking pepper bred for container growing, producing a heavy set of small, bright orange fruit that ripens sweet with almost no seed cavity. Start seed indoors 6-8 weeks before the last frost and move transplants out once the weather has warmed. The tidy, well-branched plant stays productive on a patio or balcony through the season, and ripe fruit can be eaten straight off the plant.

common_name: Burpee Garden Sown Little Big Boy Tomato

planting.note: Part of Burpee's Garden Sown line bred with cold-tolerant seed for direct sowing right around the last frost date rather than indoor starting.

directions: Little Big Boy is bred with cold-tolerant seed that germinates reliably when sown straight into garden soil instead of started indoors. Sow directly around the last frost date, thin seedlings as they establish, and stake or cage the indeterminate vines as they grow. The plant yields a steady supply of three-ounce slicers through late summer, a lower-effort option for gardeners who want to skip seed-starting trays.

common_name: Burpee Garden Sown Flying Saucer Tomato

planting.note: Part of Burpee's Garden Sown line bred with cold-tolerant seed for direct sowing around the last frost date.

directions: Flying Saucer is a paste tomato bred so its seed can be sown directly in garden soil around the last frost date instead of started indoors. The indeterminate vines need staking and produce roughly eight-ounce fruit in waves rather than a single flush, giving a long sauce-making harvest into fall. Thin seedlings after germination and keep soil evenly moist to avoid blossom-end rot on the meaty fruit.

planting.note: Start indoors for a spring crop, or sow in midsummer for a fall harvest in cooler regions.

directions: Tender Sprout is a sprouting-type broccoli grown for its long, slender side shoots rather than one central head, producing repeated harvests of foot-long stems over many weeks. Start seed indoors 4-6 weeks before the last frost, or sow a second planting in midsummer for a fall crop. Cut stems regularly once the first shoots appear to keep the plant sending up fresh growth.

planting.note: Set out potted plants in spring in well-drained, average to fertile soil in full sun.

directions: Solar Sisters is a compact black-eyed Susan bred for large, fully double, bicolor blooms on a tidy habit well suited to small borders and containers. Set out potted plants in spring in well-drained soil in full sun, and expect strong color from summer into fall once established. The dense, sturdy stems and roughly two-foot height keep this selection more restrained than open-pollinated Rudbeckia hirta, and deer tend to leave it alone.

planting.note: Plant bare roots in early spring as soon as the ground can be worked, setting the crown at soil level in well-drained, full-sun beds.

directions: Blackberry Truffle is a double-flowered coneflower with fully doubled, cherry-pink pom-pom blooms held on dark, blackberry-toned stems. Plant bare roots in spring as soon as the ground can be worked, setting the crown just at soil level in well-drained, full-sun beds. Like other double coneflowers it is grown primarily for garden display rather than open-centered blooms for seed-eating birds, but pollinators still visit for nectar through a long summer bloom season.

planting.note: Plant bare roots in early spring in rich, well-drained soil in full sun; stake tall spikes in windy sites.

directions: Highlander Moonlight is a bicolor delphinium producing pale-lilac and blue double florets packed densely along sturdy flower spikes. Plant bare roots in early spring in rich, well-drained soil in full sun, and stake the tall spikes in windy sites to protect the heavy blooms. Deadheading spent spikes can coax a second, lighter bloom later in the season, and the sturdy stems hold up well in cut arrangements.

planting.note: Direct sow once soil has warmed after the last frost date.

directions: Lemon Hedge is a branching annual sunflower bred to form a dense, continuously blooming hedge of lemon-yellow, four- to six-inch flowers rather than a single tall stem. Direct sow after the last frost once the soil has warmed, spacing plants closely along a border, fence line, or patio edge to encourage the hedge-like effect. Established plants keep producing new side blooms through summer, and leaving the last flush to go to seed brings in finches and other seed-eating birds.
